critics.title: Nino Rota
critics.quote: Rota would often fall asleep while viewing a rough cut of the film, and he would mostly ignore Fellini’s suggestions on the nature of the music the director had himself envisaged for a project.
critics.why: Rota scored Fellini's inner world rather than the footage, and largely ignored the director's musical ideas.

critics.title: Nino Rota
critics.quote: In two very different films starring Fellini’s wife Giulietta Masina – La Strada (1954) and Giulietta degli spiriti (1960) – Rota used quasi-circus music to hint at melancholic depths in Fellini’s female protagonists, deftly combining sad moods with jaunty instrumental gestures to create the bittersweet quality characteristic of so much of his film music.
critics.why: Names the pair's signature device: circus music as a mask for sadness in Masina's characters.

critics.title: Nino Rota
critics.quote: In Fellini’s films Rota’s music sometimes seems disconnected from the visual content, adding a supplementary layer of meaning. Perhaps this disconnection exists because Fellini often added Rota’s music only at a late stage of the editing and because Rota frequently adapted music from other compositions.
critics.why: Explains the music-image gap in Fellini's films by their working process: late addition and Rota's self-borrowing.

critics.title: Nino Rota – Fathers of Film Music, Part 15
critics.quote: Also notable was the fact that Fellini’s musical knowledge was quite limited, as such he trusted in Rota’s talent, and gave him broad creative control of the musical scores. A testimonial to Fellini’s trust was that he often filmed to Rota’s music so as to acquire a certain rhythm, or to create a certain atmosphere for a scene.
critics.why: Fellini ceded the music to Rota and shot scenes to his music for rhythm and mood.

critics.title: Nino Rota – Fathers of Film Music, Part 15
critics.quote: It was in the final analysis the power and facility of Rota’s music that unified Fellini’s disjointed, fragmentary narratives so as to achieve a cogent story. Without Rota, I believe Fellini would have been rendered to an obscure footnote in Italian cinematic history.
critics.why: A provocative claim: Rota's music held together Fellini's fragmentary films, and Fellini depended on it.

notes: Dyer's book and his Sight and Sound piece 'The Talented Mr. Rota' (2004) aren't openly readable online, and the La Strada review mostly repeats Lysy's earlier essay, so it's in reading only. Review pass: dropped Dyer's IKKM fellow page (a project summary, not an essay) and the Medium post (self-published), both against the brief's source rules, and Giddins' Criterion essay on La dolce vita (about the film; Rota is mentioned in passing, not the partnership). The Criterion Current post kept is a feature on Rota's score for La dolce vita; it is readable in a browser (403 to scripts), so paywalled is false.
